english: Prove that the system of all rational numbers between 0 and 1 can be mapped onto itself one-to-one and continuously (and so that a differential quotient exists), with 1/2 also corresponding to itself (i.e. so that to two [numbers] always two larger ones correspond again), only in such a way that every rational number corresponds to itself
topic: Notes on the theory of fields as a theory of the four arithmetic operations (Körper, Feld, Ring, Gitter), a claim that the only one-to-one, continuous, differentiable map of the rationals between 0 and 1 onto themselves is a linear fractional function, and the finiteness of the number of ideal classes for a field of algebraic functions of two variables.

triage.modern_statement: Let Q0 = Q ∩ (0,1), the rationals strictly between 0 and 1. Suppose f: Q0 → Q0 is a bijection that is continuous, differentiable and order-preserving (Hilbert's gloss says larger numbers go to larger numbers), and suppose f(1/2) = 1/2. Must f be the identity? The page summary states the related claim this way: the only such bijections are linear fractional (Möbius) maps x ↦ x/(x + c(1−x)) with c > 0 rational. Of these, only c = 1, the identity, fixes 1/2.
triage.answered_by: The answer is no: the claimed rigidity is false. P. Franklin (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 27 (1925), 91–100) stated that for any countable dense subsets A and B of two open intervals there is a real-analytic f with f' > 0 mapping one interval onto the other and A onto B. Gauthier (2019) found a gap in Franklin's proof, but noted that the conclusion still holds by Burke's 2009 theorem. Barth and Schneider (J. London Math. Soc. 1970) proved results of the same kind for entire functions. D. Lombardo (arXiv 1606.07012, 2016; Rend. Lincei Mat. Appl. 28 (2017), 65–83) addressed exactly this setting: he built strictly increasing analytic, non-rational maps f: [0,1] → [0,1] that restrict to bijections of Q ∩ [0,1].

evidence.claim: Franklin (1925) stated that for countable dense A and B in open intervals I and J there is a real-analytic f from I onto J with f'>0 and f(A)=B. Gauthier (2019) noted a flaw in the proof, but the conclusion still holds by Burke's 2009 theorem.
Survey of the history (Stäckel, Franklin, Barth–Schneider): Franklin used Cantor's back-and-forth method to get functions analytic near R that map one countable dense set onto another monotonically.

Barth & Schneider, 'Entire functions mapping countable dense subsets of the reals onto each other monotonically', J. London Math. Soc. (2) 2 (1970) 620–626. Cantor showed that any two countable dense real sets are order-isomorphic, and such an isomorphism can be taken to be the restriction of an entire function.
Lombardo: there exists a strictly increasing analytic function f:[0,1]→[0,1] inducing a bijection of Q∩[0,1], and such a function can be non-rational (transcendental).
Published version: D. Lombardo, 'On the analytic bijections of the rationals in [0,1]', Rend. Lincei Mat. Appl. 28 (2017), 65–83.

triage.why: Hilbert wanted to prove that a differentiable, order-preserving bijection of the rationals in (0,1) fixing 1/2 must be the identity (or, in the page summary's version, must be linear fractional). Later work shows this is false. Franklin (1925), Barth–Schneider (1970) and Lombardo (2016/17) give analytic or entire, strictly increasing maps that carry one countable dense set onto another, including bijections of Q∩[0,1] that are not linear fractional. Some of these sources say their maps can approximate any given increasing analytic function or meet extra conditions. My own check, not taken from the sources: the map can be made to fix 1/2. Glue two rational Möbius maps on [0,1/2] and [1/2,1] whose derivatives match at 1/2 (for example both equal to 2). This gives a C^1 counterexample. None of the sources links the result to Hilbert's note, and it is not one of his published problems. Related questions are still being studied: the arithmetic of such analytic bijections, and maps of countable dense sets by entire functions (including a 2026 arXiv paper on maps into C). Confidence is medium because Hilbert's handwriting is partly unclear (an '[?]' and struck-through text).
